lead: A spark-ignition engine burns its charge through a thin flame front that sweeps out from the spark plug. Flame velocity is how fast that front travels. The mass burning rate — flame front area × unburnt charge density × flame speed — decides how quickly the cylinder pressure climbs. That climb, the rate of pressure rise in bar per degree of crank angle, fixes where the peak pressure sits, how much work comes out and how close the engine is to knock. You read it directly from a pressure–crank angle trace.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.1 for the three stages of SI combustion and the ignition lag that starts the flame.

blocks.text: Combustion in a petrol engine takes place in a thin zone called the flame front, a few tenths of a millimetre thick. Behind it is burnt gas; ahead of it is unburnt charge. Reactions inside the front release heat and raise the temperature of the gas.
Flame velocity is the distance the front travels divided by the time taken. Its unit is m/s. If the front crosses 40 mm of chamber in 2 ms, the velocity is 0.040 m ÷ 0.002 s = 20 m/s.

Flame speed is the speed of the front measured normal to itself, relative to the unburnt gas just ahead of it. It is a property of the mixture, not of the engine. Flame velocity measured in a running engine is relative to the cylinder head, so it also contains the gas motion.

blocks.where: S<sub>T</sub> is the turbulent flame speed (m/s); S<sub>L</sub> is the laminar flame speed (m/s); u′ is the turbulence intensity, the rms fluctuation of gas velocity (m/s).

blocks.text: S<sub>L</sub> peaks slightly rich of stoichiometric, near an equivalence ratio φ of 1.1, where φ is the actual fuel-air ratio divided by the stoichiometric one. It rises with temperature and falls with pressure. S<sub>T</sub> is much larger because turbulence wrinkles and folds the front, so more fresh mixture meets the reaction zone every second.

sections.h3: Flame front area and mass burning rate

blocks.text: Pressure rise comes from burning mass, not from flame position. The quantity that matters is the mass burning rate, the kilograms of charge burnt per second.

blocks.where: ṁ<sub>b</sub> is the mass burning rate (kg/s); ρ<sub>u</sub> is the density of the unburnt charge (kg/m³), roughly 10 to 15 kg/m³ just before the spark in a naturally aspirated engine; A<sub>f</sub> is the flame front area (m²); S<sub>T</sub> is the turbulent flame speed (m/s).

blocks.text: A<sub>f</sub> is small at the spark, grows as the kernel becomes a sphere, and shrinks again when the front reaches the walls and the piston crown. Because the flame first grows and then dies, the burning rate peaks around the middle of combustion and tails off near the end.
This is why chamber shape matters. A compact chamber with the spark near the centre lets the front sweep a short path with a large area for most of the burn. See Chapter 3.8 for chamber layouts.
The rate of pressure rise is how fast cylinder pressure changes with crank angle, written dp/dθ in bar per degree of crank angle (°CA). Over an interval it is the average slope of the pressure trace.

blocks.where: p<sub>1</sub> and p<sub>2</sub> are cylinder pressures (bar) at crank angles θ<sub>1</sub> and θ<sub>2</sub> (°CA, measured from TDC, top dead centre).

blocks.text: The first law of thermodynamics for the cylinder gives the instantaneous value.

blocks.where: γ is the ratio of specific heats of the gas, about 1.35; V is the instantaneous cylinder volume (m³); dQ/dt is the heat release rate (W), roughly ṁ<sub>b</sub> × the lower calorific value of the fuel; p is the cylinder pressure (Pa).

blocks.text: The first term is combustion and the second is piston motion. Volume sits in the denominator of both. The same heat released into a larger volume raises the pressure less. That is the trap in this chapter: high flame speed alone does not give a high rate of pressure rise.
A normal SI engine peaks at about 1 to 2 bar/°CA. Knocking cycles reach several times this, which is what produces the sharp pressure spike and the metallic noise; Chapter 3.3 takes that up.

Fast burn pushes the peak pressure nearer TDC. More of the heat is released at small volume, so more of it becomes work and efficiency goes up, and the end gas has less time to self-ignite. Too fast a burn, however, loads the piston and bearings and makes the engine noisy. Sluggish burn puts the peak late, wastes heat to the exhaust and runs hot.

figure.caption: The slope of the line joining the two measured points is the average rate of pressure rise: 30 bar over 15° of crank angle, that is 2 bar per degree. A steeper line would mean a faster burn and a peak pressure nearer TDC.

spec.aria: Line from 10 degrees after TDC at 30 bar to 25 degrees after TDC at 60 bar; its slope is the average rate of pressure rise.

examples.question: In an SI engine test, the cylinder pressure is 30 bar at 10° aTDC and 60 bar at 25° aTDC. (a) Find the average rate of pressure rise in bar/°CA. (b) The engine runs at 3000 rpm. Convert the answer to bar/ms.
steps: Read the two points: p₁ = 30 bar at θ₁ = 10° aTDC, p₂ = 60 bar at θ₂ = 25° aTDC.
Pressure interval: Δp = p₂ − p₁ = 60 − 30 = 30 bar.
Crank angle interval: Δθ = θ₂ − θ₁ = 25 − 10 = 15 °CA.
Average rate of pressure rise = Δp / Δθ = 30 bar / 15 °CA = 2 bar/°CA.
Time for one revolution at 3000 rpm = 60 s / 3000 = 0.02 s. One revolution is 360°, so one degree takes 0.02 / 360 = 5.556 × 10⁻⁵ s = 0.05556 ms.
Rate in bar/ms = 2 bar/°CA ÷ 0.05556 ms/°CA = 36 bar/ms.
Check by the other route: 3000 rpm = 50 rev/s = 18 000 °/s. Then 2 bar/° × 18 000 °/s = 36 000 bar/s = 36 bar/ms.
examples.answer: The average rate of pressure rise is 2 bar per degree of crank angle, which equals 36 bar per millisecond at 3000 rpm.
examples.check:
p1, th1 = 30.0, 10.0
p2, th2 = 60.0, 25.0
N = 3000.0
dpdtheta = (p2 - p1) / (th2 - th1)
ms_per_deg = 1000.0 / (6.0 * N)
dpdt = dpdtheta / ms_per_deg
print(round(dpdtheta, 4))
print(round(ms_per_deg, 4))
print(round(dpdt, 4))

traps: A high flame speed alone does not fix the rate of pressure rise. Mass burning rate (density × flame area × flame speed) and chamber volume also control it.
bar/°CA, bar/ms and bar/s are different units. At N rpm one degree takes 1000/(6N) ms, so 2 bar/°CA is 36 bar/ms at 3000 rpm but 24 bar/ms at 2000 rpm.
Flame speed is measured relative to the unburnt gas; flame velocity in the engine is measured relative to the cylinder head. Do not use the two words interchangeably in a definition question.
The slope read between two points is the average rate; the peak instantaneous rate is higher and occurs near the middle of the burn.
Quoting S<sub>L</sub> = 20 m/s is wrong. That order of magnitude belongs to the turbulent flame speed; laminar values are below 1 m/s.

quiz.q: Define flame velocity and give its unit.
quiz.a: Flame velocity is the distance travelled by the flame front divided by the time taken. Unit: m/s.

quiz.q: Why is the turbulent flame speed several times the laminar flame speed in a running engine?
quiz.a: Turbulence wrinkles and folds the front, so a larger area of fresh mixture contacts the reaction zone each second. A simple model gives S<sub>T</sub> ≈ S<sub>L</sub> + u′, where u′ is the turbulence intensity.

quiz.q: Cylinder pressure is 25 bar at 8° aTDC and 55 bar at 22° aTDC. Find the average rate of pressure rise.
quiz.a: Δp = 55 − 25 = 30 bar; Δθ = 22 − 8 = 14 °CA. Average rate = 30/14 = 2.14 bar/°CA.

quiz.q: An engine at 2000 rpm shows an average rate of pressure rise of 2 bar/°CA. Express it in bar/ms.
quiz.a: One degree takes 1000/(6 × 2000) = 0.0833 ms. Rate = 2/0.0833 = 24 bar/ms.

quiz.q: Two engines release the same heat at the same rate, but one has a larger cylinder volume at that crank angle. Which shows the lower rate of pressure rise, and why?
quiz.a: The engine with the larger volume. In dp/dt = ((γ − 1)/V)·dQ/dt − (γp/V)·dV/dt, volume is in the denominator, so the same heat release produces a smaller pressure rise when V is larger.

quiz.q: A high flame speed alone does not guarantee a fast rate of pressure rise. Explain with the mass burning rate formula.
quiz.a: ṁ<sub>b</sub> = ρ<sub>u</sub>·A<sub>f</sub>·S<sub>T</sub>. If the flame front area is small or the unburnt density is low, the mass burnt per second stays small even at high S<sub>T</sub>, and the chamber volume further dilutes the pressure rise.

quiz.q: What does the slope of a pressure–crank angle trace give?
quiz.a: The rate of pressure rise, in bar per degree of crank angle.

quiz.q: Why does fast burn raise efficiency but also raise mechanical loading?
quiz.a: Fast burn puts peak pressure nearer TDC, so more heat is converted to work and less goes to the exhaust. The same fast rise means a steeper pressure curve, which loads the piston, rings and bearings and raises noise.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production engines are developed with piezoelectric pressure transducers that sample every 0.1° of crank, and the burn is summarised by the crank angles at which 10% and 90% of the mass has burnt. Heat release analysis converts the measured pressure trace into dQ/dθ using the first law given above. Flame speed correlations for different fuels feed 3-D CFD models that predict knock before a metal engine is built. Search terms to follow: mass fraction burned, heat release analysis, turbulent flame speed correlation, cylinder pressure measurement.
